newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway says rate cuts call for tight budget.
newsitem.headline: Norway says rate cuts call for tight budget.

text.p: Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg said on Tuesday that last week's Norwegian interest rate cuts made it important to maintain a tight budget in order to keep inflation down.

Stoltenberg, who switched from being energy minister to finance minister in new Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland's government last month, also reiterated that there would be no switch in Norway's economic policy.

Speaking to foreign correspondents, he painted a rosy picture of the economy, which is projected to show a surplus of 40.9 billion crowns in 1997 -- the third consecutive year that the oil-rich country will have a budget surplus.

But Stoltenberg said there were warning signs the economy could become overheated and that last Wednesday's cut in key interest rates by 0.5 percentage points made it even more important to maintain a tight budget and fiscal policy.
"Lower rates can incease domestic demand," he said. "That is why this must be compensated for through a tight fiscal policy."

The central bank cut the rates in an effort to rein in the crown, which has strengthened rapidly recently partly because of the wide gap in interest-rate differentials between Norway and other European markets and also because of high oil prices.
Norway, which pumps three million barrels of oil per day, is the world's second largest crude exporter after Saudi Arabia.
"There is a danger the Norwegian economy can get too high a temperature, that the growth becomes too strong," Stoltenberg said. "There are warning lamps blinking.

"We have strong consumption growth of about four percent, growth in bank lending, a pretty strong growth in real estate prices, an explosive new-car registration and the strongest real term wage growth for 20 years.

"There is a danger the economy will take off. That is why we have presented a budget that calls for a tightening of the Norwegian economy of about one percent of Gross National Product (GDP)," he said.

The Labour minority government has said it will keep a tight grip on expenditure for fear of fuelling inflation, but the opposition in parliament is seeking to spend more of the oil money on areas such as health. The draft budget will be adopted in December.

"This is a minority government and it has always had to accept changes to the budget," Stoltenberg said. "There will be changes this year, too. But there are different kinds of changes. We have a dialogue going about investing more in health care but it has to be covered by other means than the petroleum fund."
The government is saving the surplus in a state petroleum fund to help pay for pensions for future generations once the oil and gas resources run out some time next century.
